evidence.text: An ox's horned head
Pictograph of the head of a cow.
大牲也。牛，件也；件，事理也。象角頭三、封㞑之形。凡牛之屬皆从牛。

Pictogram (象形) of a bull's head, with two horns and two ears. Perhaps unrelated to 告; unrelated to 先.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ŋwə.

evidence.field: 字形演變；字形來源說明
evidence.text: The entry lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen materials for 牛. Its explanation says the graph emphasizes the ox’s head and horns and originally referred to the animal. The sequence is a record of graphic forms; the page does not provide dates for each listed specimen in the inspected text.
evidence.title: 漢字「牛」：字形演變

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, Shuowen Jiezi entry and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The entry transmits Xu Shen’s account: “大牲也” and describes the graph as depicting horns, head, and a raised back/tail feature. Duan Yucai disputes the transmitted gloss and proposes “事也。理也,” explaining 牛 through its work and the dissectible patterns of the animal. This is a historical lexicographic interpretation and later commentary, not independent confirmation of the graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「牛」

evidence.source: Unicode Consortium, Unicode Standard, CJK Radicals Supplement names list
evidence.text: Unicode identifies ⺧ as a variant of Kangxi radical 93 and points to 牛 U+725B; this concerns the radical form and does not establish the ancient graphic history of 牛.
evidence.title: CJK Radicals Supplement

evidence.text: The entry displays 牛 under oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen headings. It describes the form as emphasizing the ox’s head and horns and says its original meaning was the animal 牛. The page does not date individual specimens.
evidence.title: 漢字「牛」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database says oracle-bone and bronze forms depict a frontal ox head with two curved horns; its account notes that Shang bronze forms also show ears, eyes, and nose. It gives the inscriptional phrase 友簋「易（賜）牛三」 as an example of 牛 referring to cattle, and notes personal-name use in bronze inscriptions. These statements report the database’s analyses and examples; they do not independently date the cited inscription here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析「牛」

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi, 牛 entry, as transcribed by Shuowen.org
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry calls 牛 a large sacrificial animal and describes the graph in terms of horns, head, and tail. Duan Yucai offers a different gloss in his commentary. These are historical lexicographic interpretations, not independent proof of the graph’s formation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「牛」

evidence.text: The basic entry lists animal, figurative stubbornness, a lunar mansion, an abbreviation for 牽牛星, zodiac animal, a traditional lunar-calendar day, and surname among its senses. This undated modern dictionary list cannot establish when those extensions arose.
evidence.title: 漢字「牛」：基本資料

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.
